plan: In this second-price auction format, the dominant strategy is to bid my true value, since I pay the second-highest bid (not my own bid) if I win. My value is $0, meaning any positive price I'd pay for winning would result in a loss. Bidding above $0 risks winning and paying more than $0, leading to negative profit. Bidding exactly $0 ensures I either don't win (profit = $0) or in the rare case of winning with all bids at $0, I still profit $0. This is optimal.

This is a second-price sealed-bid auction with independent private values. In such auctions, bidding your true value is a weakly dominant strategy regardless of the number of competitors, since you pay the second-highest bid (not your own) if you win. Overbidding risks winning at a price above value, while underbidding risks losing profitable opportunities. With no repeated learning needed since values are redrawn independently, the optimal strategy is straightforward: bid exactly my private value of $30.

In a second-price auction, bidding your true value is the dominant strategy regardless of what others do. Since I only pay the second-highest bid if I win, bidding above my value risks paying more than the item is worth, and bidding below reduces my chance of winning a profitable auction. With a value of $8, the optimal bid is simply $8, ensuring I maximize expected profit given the strategic properties of second-price auctions.
